Chloe Smith
THR 141-002
October 9, 2023

Habits and Process

I have noted many mental/personal habits, of varying types. When it comes to working with a team, I often wait to be told what the vision is before making choices in a show. I also have a tenement to not talk to castmates out of fear that they won't agree with my interpretation - or simply won't mesh with my process. The “I’ve never prepared enough” mentality also has plagued me for many years; in every project I do, I feel unprepared, whether I've worked hard or not. 

Sometimes I struggle to move forward with the work before I really understand and connect with the story. While I always eventually want to get to a place where I’m super comfortable with the story, it’s detrimental when I feel like I can’t move forward until I understand deeply. 

As an actor, I've been told I often make quick emotional turns on stage - I differentiate my different thoughts, tactics, or feelings too sharply, with no fluidity. I also either push too hard and try to make my choices obvious, or I don’t allow specificity out of a fear of doing too much (I do all of my instincts/choices at 50%). In addition I tend to make every character I play like me in at least some way, whether it be physicality, personality, or beliefs.  

Some physical habits I’ve found relate to the mental/personal habits. When I don’t know how to tell the story with my body, I stiffen. Stiff body, shoulders tense and high, arms apparently relaxed but immobile… between fight, flight, and freeze, i choose freeze as my response when I don't know what to do. 

Because of this “what do I do” fear, I developed a habit that my hands always have to have a “home base” before I’m comfortable with a character, even if that’s just deciding that home base is by my sides. I’ve also noticed that I have a habit at times of walking at unnatural speeds. Going too fast, I’ll march straight to the next place in my blocking, walking quickly and then stopping abruptly. Alternatively, I’ll go too slow, uncomfortably sauntering, feeling almost like I’m telegraphing every step I take. 

However, when I’m not overthinking what to do physically, my habits are actually quite the opposite. Like the quick emotional turns I make, I’ve been told I actually make quick physical movements and turns on stage. I also use lots of gestures and even start leaning toward another person when I’m trying to connect with them or “portray big emotions” (never a good idea to try to do that!)  

As a singer—and much less so now than it used to be—I shake my head when I sing, and I think especially at the ends of phrases. 

Now, while most of these habits I am listing have been around for years, I recently made some changes in how I tend to use my physical body in performance. I made the change because it seemed to be quite effective most of the time, but it has its own dangers. I've stopped almost all physical movements, taking them, reducing them, and putting it all in the eyes. This has the potential to cut me off from choices that read well on stage, and it also plays into the habit I already have of my eyes moving around too much. Afraid to hold eye contact too long, I let my eyes dart around the stage. This is a very dangerous habit when I’m trying to tell the entire story with my eyes.

Lastly, I noted a “reaction” tendency in myself (this isn’t a habit, but like some of the aural things that we discussed, it’s an important reaction to realize that my body physically has regarding how I will perform on stage.) Though there aren’t many circumstances where I will be cold when performing, when I’m even a little cold I start shivering pretty soon and quite intensely. This could be important to realise for things like outdoor theatre.

Orally, I have several habits that have bothered me for quite a long time. Getting very quiet in intimate scenes, I can become inaudible for an audience at a distance. In general, my vowels get lazy easily and I slur words together, particularly when I’m tired. Another unfortunate reaction I have to the cold is that when I’m very cold it’s actually harder to enunciate - it almost feels like my tongue muscles get numb from the cold. 

I have a tendency to rush overall when I’m working with new material. But the long pauses will still exist between thoughts, so that I can MAKE SURE the audience knows that there’s punctuation or a shift in thought. 

I have a tendency when “chewing words” or trying to get the most out of them to go towards the consonants instead of the vowels. 

In my own life I have some speech habits I’ve noticed. These include frequent use of “Like,” “Girrrrrrl,” “Frick” and other fake expletives (I pretty much swear like a sailor … but with fake swears. Seriously. Yes, it’s kind of embarrassing.) I talk so fast I misspeak, and I laugh at my own jokes to make sure people know they’re a joke).

My aural reactions and habits are kind of random, but: I get super freaked out by too much bagpipe, by Arabic music (think microtonal maqam scales), and by too heavy drums when I’m physically close enough to them to feel the vibrations in my chest.

Probably a more common aural habit/reaction I have is the way I respond to music. Music in a rehearsal context almost inevitably changes how I move and how I see the atmosphere of a scene or exploration. This is mostly quality-based: if it’s uptempo it may affect my tempo directly, but otherwise it’s more about the feeling that the music evokes and how my whole mind and body respond to that new quality and atmosphere. 

Overall process for the Electra monologue:
Explore the literal text
Explore orally and aurally
Note assonance and consonance
Explore thoughts in the text 
Track logically
Create a clear understanding of structure within the piece
Dive further into given circumstances; take notes on what you need to
Explore text in character
What does each phrase mean to her
How do the words present themselves to her in the moment
Does she ever need to search for the word
Specify text in character
What is the purpose of each phrase
Add verb tactics to each segment
Work through given circumstances and actions
Practice these actions with a moment before and scenic objective
Specify actions further if needed 
Adding qualities, Laban efforts, subtext, etc.
Release
Experience this moment with the invisible scene partner, focusing on that person, not my actions of choices I've worked on 
Repeat any steps needed, interspersing each step explored with practicing the given circumstances and the release

What will I do to acknowledge and either work with or address these habits or reactions I have identified?
Make choices right away even if I'm not “told to”
Be very specific with the underlying story, then push nothing (no emphasizing my choices to be sure the audience got it)
Trust the preparation at each stage of the process
Assess similarities and differences between me and the character; decide if i actually want them to be that way
Practice entire thing totally still
Practice entire thing totally relaxed 
Practice entire thing with as big body as possible, acting totally on impulse
Not collapsing spine
Play with eye contact staying totally engaged, moving a lot, experiment with what actually works
Focus on enjoying the vowels in my mouth
Keeping the idea of Shakespeare’s enjambed lines - where you don't really have time to stop between thoughts because there is still more you need to say
Keeping full breath and resonance even if the “quiet” or more contained moments
Maybe try practice this while listening to several different types of music to see how it may inform the piece or not Chloe Smith

Production Laboratory

March 8, 2024


Love’s Labour’s Lost Reflection Paper


How do I even begin to reflect on one of the most life-changing show experiences I’ve ever had? This show changed me, I think. So let’s just take it chronologically:


I knew that my number one goal prior to rehearsals starting was to come in completely off-book and totally understanding what every line meant. I know for myself that if I don’t memorize to word-perfect right away, I will keep paraphrasing throughout the whole process. Thus, I decided that my goal would be to be truly word-perfect before we even started rehearsals. Although I certainly didn’t do it perfectly every single time in rehearsal, I did know every line word-for-word before we began! I also did go through and make sure that I understood every single word before we started rehearsals. I think some of the specificity of that got lost after an initial read through – there were a couple words that I forgot what they meant and had to go look again. But I did come in understanding what I was saying, including the Latin. I’m really glad I did both of these goals, because it gave me a great foundation to play with from the very beginning.


It turned out that it was useful to really understand the material before the first rehearsal since we did, in fact, jump straight into a walk-through on the first day, letting our preliminary understanding of the text and initial impulses have their heyday before we started blocking. As soon as I heard that we would be doing that, I knew that I had to go ahead and make big choices. I actually took my inspiration from past castmates with whom I have done Shakespearean comedy. I have always aspired to the level of play and freedom that my friends from Shakespeare in the Valley used in our rehearsals. The philosophy we used at The Valley was that there is no such thing as a rehearsal; every time you do it, it’s its own performance (a similar ideology to the “performance energy always” that we talk about at RTC). So when MRK said that we should jump in and make it look as though it was a fully blocked show already, I knew that I needed to take that mentality and channel all the comedic enthusiasm of my The Valley friends who played the really comedic roles during my summer there. And I’m so glad I did! It showed me from the beginning how fun my choices could be when I just jumped in and had a good time.


Now if only I had been able to keep that level of confidence and not-overthinking throughout the whole process! The first week of rehearsal was magical; I felt like everything was coming together so brilliantly and vibrantly, I felt so funny and confident, and I just loved the people and the process. But as the weeks went on I felt like I wasn’t making a ton of forward progress and was maybe even going backward. The laugh lines weren’t landing anymore (because of course that’s what happens when people have heard the same joke a million times) and even though I knew the jokes weren't for the cast but for the audience, I started to wonder if I just wasn't funny at all.


Up to the very end of the process I kept feeling like I was still coming up so short of what I wanted to do. I had a talk with MRK during tech and just explained that I didn't feel like I was really doing anything, like I wasn't funny. He said that I had actually gotten to a “good enough” place earlier in the process than most - early enough, perhaps, that I was just struggling with the feeling of flatlining in the work. Which, I think, he was right about. I wanted it to get better every single rehearsal, but instead it was pretty much staying the same. That bored me. I wanted to change it up, wanted to be better, wanted to get the laughs that I had gotten at the beginning of the process that had worn off now. But it wasn't changing, and I was getting frustrated. MRK told me that it just needed an audience for the magic to happen. He literally stated in it DnD terms: a spell requires verbal, physical, and somatic elements to be cast. We’d had the verbal and physical elements for a while now, he said, but it needed the somatic element of the audience to lift off its feet and actually be something. And I asked, will it? Will it be wonderful once the last element is there? I don’t want it to be “good enough”. I want it to be amazing. And he said: “I don’t know. I hope so. I guess we’ll get an audience and see.” 


And that was it. It was somehow groundbreaking for me to realize that even my beloved director, my director who I so completely admired and trusted, was living with the uncertainty too. That he was willing to live in that horribly scary, dangerous world of art: the true unknown when you make big choices. Even he couldn’t know for sure whether it would land. Somehow I think that gave me a little measure of freedom. I no longer could keep fighting for some validation, some external promise that I would be a perfect little actress and stun the audience. I had to trust the process, trust my director, and play the play. And we’d see together if it worked out.


And, indeed, I think it did.


Now let’s reflect a little on what did work for me in this process and what didn’t–and what I learned.


I think in general when I felt best about my performance was when I really dropped into the given circumstances and felt what it was to exist inside this character's body. I experimented with how I could physically affect myself into a “drunk state” without playing drunk in a fake, overblown-looking way. I suppose it helped that my actual personality is to act a little sloppy and fearless when I’m overtired! So usually the further we got into a rehearsal day and the more tired I became, the more I could drop into the silliness and lack of inhibition that mirrored the physical and mental state of the character. Generally I would break down the characteristics of how I played drunk as 1) physical: a lack of balance by feeling like my head was literally swirling around, 2) the mental state of just not caring about what I did, acting on impulse, having fun, being silly. The sweet spot seemed to be almost a lethargy and extreme energy at the same time - like a sloppy and dizzy exuberance. The more I leaned deep into this physical and mental state, the more I felt like I was really listening and responding in the scene. It somehow increased my presence and ability to work on the pinch and ouch, it seems.


There are some things I don’t know if they would have been helpful but I wonder about. These are less regrets but more opportunities for curiosity about my process. Though I understood and memorized my lines, what I didn’t do as much before the process began was scoring. I don’t know that it would’ve been helpful to create a ton of given circumstances before rehearsal started, but I do think the little more exploratory scoring might have been helpful. I certainly did start to do that, and I actually got pretty deep into my first scene with exploratory scoring (by exploratory, I mean everything from noticing initial alliteration to repetition to scansion). It wasn’t a fully realized score though, and what I really wish is that I had done more of the later scenes as well. Again, a lot of the Stanislavski work had to wait until I knew more of the story in the world that we were working in, but I wish I had at least done more Shakey scoring beforehand to really understand the complexities of the text itself. Again, all of this is within the context of a perfect world, and I’m actually really glad that I got as much done ahead of time as I did. I just know it could always be better!


Now there are some things I do actively wish I had done differently: I think the number one biggest thing that held me back in this process was the idea that my character’s whole purpose is to be funny. Which, to a large extent, it really is. But when I look back over it all, I realize that Shakespeare, in his brilliance, writes stories that are cohesively powerful, and the truth is that part of what my character does is illuminate, from a different side, the “absurdity of learning for its own sake”. To be clear, I do not actually believe that learning for its own sake is bad at all; I love it personally and think it can be so deeply enriching. Nor do I believe that Shakespeare believed that. But I do think that a big point of the plot of Love’s Labour’s Lost is to show that compared to relationships, studying just to be smart is not important. All this to say, I think that Holofernes and Sir Nathaniel are very much part of the greater purpose of telling that story. We simply offer a different element of that story, showing, particularly, how silly it is to think you're superior to anyone else because you have more academic knowledge. 


Thus, there is a reason that the characters must be grounded in truthful choices and given circumstances. In addition, even comedy with no other purpose doesn’t land without truth behind it. I struggled so much with this throughout. I knew I needed real objectives and tactics, and while I do think that these were present, I wish so much that I had relied on them more. As I mentioned in talkbacks, I think that I probably would have been less in my head about whether I was funny or not had I been focused instead on getting what I needed tactically. Had I a more solid Stanislavski grounding, with strong given circumstances and true driving need or a tactical pursuit, it would have opened me as an actor. But I was somehow afraid of leaning too far into it. I think I was scared that it would remove me from the world of storytelling that we had created - that it would lead to me to make new (and undoubtedly more truthful) choices that were different from what we had already set for blocking or for the intention of a given line. Yes, I was afraid to do more of what would have made me more truthful because I didn't want to change things that we had set in rehearsal. I do recognize that this is truly ridiculous, especially because one of the mantras of this process was “retain the capacity to surprise even yourself.” I’m so angry that I got scared and stuck in my choices so early in the process despite all the warnings against it. It does make me especially glad that I forced myself to make big, bold choices really early in the process, since I think they drove a lot of what ended up being part of the final show. However, I feel like I lost that ability to make big choices so early. Feeling stuck with the blocking that we had, I couldn’t even make any more truthful, better character choices than I had, because oh no, what if they messed up the blocking? Or the original intention I had with that line? 


All of this to say, I wish so much that I had just forced myself to take it all so literally and un-comedically, even if it was just stepping into the “classroom feel” for a day and working my Stanislavski score fully and with not a hint of added comedic effect, pretending that I was in John’s freshman acting class. I think if I had let myself play it so incredibly seriously a few times, I would have found a lot of truth that I honestly think I never found. Yes, I do think I found more truth by the end of the process, but I really believe there could have been more. And I really wanted to still make new surprising choices throughout. I believe it might have been an overall much better performance if I had. Perhaps I could have actually been more funny by being more truthful and also gotten out of my own way by getting out of my head. In sum, I think that my fear held me back deeply, and I realize in retrospect how silly it was to let that control me so much.


There were some other interesting things that I noticed in the process. Living in a character with physical, mental, and vocal choices, layering on the drunkenness, and then trying to hit each moment clearly with my scene partners was rather complicated! My goal was less for the audience to understand every single word and much more that they would understand the story. I knew that if I deeply understood every single word that I was saying and why I was saying it, the meaning would come through. After all, I believe that the story included the literal events happening in the scene as well as who my character was and the relationships between the characters/how they evolved. The biggest struggle was in portraying my character himself. For so much of the process, I didn’t really understand how he was supposed to present himself. I think I understood who he was inside: that he was really intellectual, loved studying and all of these academic pursuits, and also loved to have a good time (and at this exact moment was in party mode instead of academic mode). While some of the specificity of that I had to work through – how much did he care about things being proper and up to snuff academically while in party mode, for example – I think I understood the basis. But I really didn’t understand how to present him physically and vocally. I think that some of the choices that I made towards the beginning of the process felt more truthful to the character that I thought I was supposed to be playing, so when I removed those choices, I felt it lost some specificity and clarity. The one big choice that I had most regrets about over the course of the process was that I, despite my best intentions, memorized the lines with the pseudo-British accent that I carried through the first couple rehearsals. As I got notes and direction on the character, even though he never said not to use the accent, he didn’t use the accent when giving me new lines and giving me intentions for lines, so I just assumed I had to remove it. I regret not actually asking. However, I also think that I attached too much of my perception of character around this one external thing that I thought summed up the character really well: the silly affected voice. I think I had thereby connected many of the underlying character choices that I was subconsciously making with the voice, removing those choices once I didn’t have it. Perhaps it was even that I didn’t remove those subconscious character choices, but I felt like I had because I missed the external symbol. It took me pretty much the whole process to regain confidence in my character choices without that silly affected voice.


I certainly experienced so much more struggle in this work than I expected. I thought I knew Shakespeare so well, yet I had to look up every other word Holofernes says. I had only three scenes, yet I have rarely struggled so much to complete and feel confident about a solid Stanislavski score for any piece I’ve done. I thought I knew so much about acting as a senior, yet I have rarely felt so disappointed in my own work and ability to approach material through clear and informed technique. Yes, this process challenged me deeply. However, it was also one of the best show processes I have EVER been involved in, and I have been acting since I was six years old. It made me question so much of what I was doing and challenged me endlessly, but it also gave me a new kind of confidence in who I am as an actor, who I am in the rehearsal room, and the kinds of relationships I can have with my castmates. It reminded me how much fun acting can be. It showed me how many of my skills I can use in this industry. It showed me how to be incredibly professional and have so much fun at the same time. It reminded me that the little nerd inside me is so welcome in this world. It made me feel special, and silly, and myself. It also, in some weird, indirect ways, has slowly helped me actually believe that I belong in this industry. I can’t even begin to express how much this frightened little senior BFA needed to be told that in the slow, sweet, gentle ways I was through this process and the people I worked with in it. I think the biggest area of growth for me was truly the openness it has created and is creating in me. I am willing to be wrong. I can admit that honestly, I felt like I didn't know what I was doing so much of the time. It has humbled me. AND… it has given me enormous confidence, has encouraged me to make crazy choices and be my crazy self. I know I grew as a performer, particularly a performer of comedy. But I think mostly, I grew as a person.


In summary, I think my biggest takeaways are that I will, indeed, have a different process for every single show I do, but I also can trust that the basic work we do can apply to anything, even if it’s something incredibly foreign, new, and scary. I hope to use this knowledge to bring the simple clarity of Stanislavski work to future comedy that I do in a more committed manner. I hope to trust myself and my fellow artists more and allow the uncertainty to be a part of the process. I hope to keep making new choices and truly retain the capacity to surprise even myself through the entirety of whatever process I do next (within my permission as a cast member) - and I hope to retain the capacity to do so in my life forever. I want to be “louder, faster, funnier”! I want to love wholeheartedly and bring kinship and joy to every rehearsal process I’m part of. Genuinely, I think that the most important takeaway I have from this process is not even about acting. It’s about the rehearsal room and the kind of community I want to exist in my creative spaces.


Oh, what a profound delight to be a part of the story of this show! I think we did it. We made this place our home.



Task:


This was a very significant year for me in terms of taking all the work I had done over three previous years and coalescing the whole of it into my own process. 

It’s hard to get perspective while it’s happening, but looking back, what was my comparative confidence level in my overall ability as an actor between semesters?

Based on your two documents, your comparative confidence level in your overall ability as an actor increased dramatically from the first semester (Fall 2023) to the second semester (Spring 2024).

Here is a breakdown of the comparison:

### **First Semester (Fall 2023) - Low Confidence**

Your "Habits and Process" document from October 9, 2023, reveals a state of deep self-scrutiny and low confidence. You catalogued a long list of perceived flaws, both mental and physical, that you felt were holding you back as an actor. These included:

*   **Mental/Personal Insecurities:** Waiting for direction, fear of disagreement with castmates, a persistent feeling of being unprepared, difficulty moving forward without absolute certainty, making overly sharp emotional shifts, and a tendency to either overplay or underplay choices.
*   **Physical Habits:** Stiffening and freezing when uncertain, unnatural walking speeds, and a habit of conveying emotion entirely through your eyes to the point of distraction.
*   **Oral/Aural Issues:** Becoming inaudible, lazy diction, rushing lines, and distracting speech patterns in your daily life.

The overall tone of this document is one of self-criticism and a desire to fix fundamental problems. You were in a phase of identifying weaknesses, indicating a lack of confidence in your established process and abilities.

### **Second Semester (Spring 2024) - Significantly Higher Confidence**

Your "Love’s Labour’s Lost Reflection Paper" from March 8, 2024, details a transformative journey that culminated in a profound boost in confidence. While you experienced a dip in confidence mid-process (feeling unfunny and stuck), the overall arc led to a powerful realization of your growth.

*   **Initial Confidence:** You began the rehearsal process with a clear goal and achieved it (being off-book and understanding the text), which provided a strong foundation.
*   **The Struggle:** Your confidence wavered during rehearsals as jokes wore out and you felt you weren't progressing. You were frustrated and in your head.
*   **The Breakthrough:** A pivotal conversation with your director, MRK, helped you accept uncertainty and trust the process. You realized that even your director didn't have all the answers, which freed you from seeking external validation.
*   **The Transformation:** By the end of the process, you explicitly state that the experience **"has given me enormous confidence,"** **"encouraged me to make crazy choices,"** and **"in some weird, indirect ways, has slowly helped me actually believe that I belong in this industry."** You describe the process as one of the best you've ever had, stating, **"I know I grew as a performer,"** and that the biggest takeaway was the openness and confidence you gained.

### **Conclusion**

Comparing the two semesters, your confidence level shifted from being low and fraught with self-doubt to being significantly higher and more resilient. The first semester reflects an actor actively grappling with insecurity, while the second semester's reflection celebrates a hard-won confidence built through a challenging but ultimately triumphant artistic journey. You went from listing your flaws to recognizing your growth and believing in your place in the industry.

Break down any habits I spoke of with different tone between the two documents. Differentiate into my opinions of the habits themselves changing versus my opinion of my own work or ability changing.
